newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's Bucaram seen losing shaky grip on power.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's Bucaram seen losing shaky grip on power.

text.p: Ecuador's defence minister resigned on Saturday amid reports that the military had withdrawn all support from the government of embattled President Abdala Bucaram.
"General Victor Bayas has resigned the post of defence minister," the ministry said in a statement.
It gave no reason for the retired army general's sudden decision to join three other cabinet officials, including Energy Minister Alfredo Adum, who have walked out on Bucaram in the last 48 hours.

But it said Bayas, who declared a nationwide state of emergency on Friday to quell anti-Bucaram protests, had issued a call for "peace and order" amid the country's deepening political crisis and urged Ecuadoreans to avoid "excesses that could have lamentable consequences."

Bucaram, who left the heavy fortified presidential palace in Quito late on Friday for his traditional power base in Guayaquil, dismissed Thursday's vote by Congress deposing him on grounds of mental incompetence. He called it an attempted coup and said he had no intention of stepping down.

But national radio said he had lost all support from the military, which handed over power to a civilian government in 1979 but remains a powerful behind-the-scenes player in the political life of this tiny South American country.
"Bucaram no longer has the support of the military high command," Radio Quito said in news bulletin, citing what it said were sources close to senior military officials.
The report could not be immediately confirmed.
Three top politicians, including Bucaram, who is popularly known as "El Loco" or "madman," have been vying for Ecuador's top job since Thursday night.
The other contenders are Vice President Rosalia Arteaga and congressional leader Fabian Alarcon, who was named acting president by Congress.

The military has vowed to maintain a neutral stance, and has fallen short so far of backing either Alarcon, Arteaga or Bucaram. But many analysts see it as playing a crucial role in choosing Bucaram's possible successor and ending the deepening constitutional conflict.

Bucaram -- who served as mayor of Guayaquil in the 1980s -- staged what looked like a triumphant return to the city late on Friday after abandoning the ornate Carondelet presidential palace for the first time since Thursday's vote.

At an impromptu news conference, which appeared to draw more well-wishers than reporters, the populist candidate who won a solid victory in most of Ecuador's 21 provinces before taking office just six months ago, said democracy would cease to exist without him.

"Abdala represents democracy, anything else would be a coup," he said. He also challenged Alarcon to demonstrate his "manhood" by meeting him in Guayaquil late on Saturday to thrash out their political differences face-to-face.

Alarcon, who led thousands of supporters in an aborted attempt to storm the presidential palace on Friday in which an 18-year-old student was killed, responded to the challenge by likening Bucaram to a punchy and "foul-mouthed" boxer looking to slug it out in a ring that was crumbling beneath him.
"This isn't a question of boxers having to climb into the ring (with him)," Alarcon said. He dismissed any chance of a meeting with Bucaram or talks aimed at ironing out their differences in private.
After the clash at the palace with riot police on Friday, Alarcon announced that he was beginning an indefinite hunger strike to force Bucaram from power.
